claims.text: Adding 2–6 at.% Ge to a Ti- and Ni-primary high-entropy alloy will induce fine precipitates.
The Ge-induced precipitates will pin grain boundaries.
Ge promotes precipitate nucleation during solidification or subsequent elevated-temperature exposure.
Ge-induced microstructural features will refine and stabilize the grain structure.
Grain-boundary pinning will restrict grain growth.
The proposed grain refinement and stabilization will reduce dislocation mobility.
The Ge-doped alloy will have higher elevated-temperature yield strength than the Ge-free Ti-Ni-primary alloy.
The Ge-doped alloy will have higher hardness than the Ge-free alloy.
The Ge-doped alloy will have improved elevated-temperature creep resistance and a lower creep strain rate than the Ge-free alloy.
The fine-precipitate mechanism will remain active at operating temperatures up to about 1000 °C.
The target high-entropy composition requires every constituent, including Ge, to be present at approximately 5–35 at.%.
Interactions with other alloying elements may alter Ge-induced precipitate formation.

contradictions.description: The intervention permits 2–6 at.% Ge, whereas the stated high-entropy boundary requires each element to be approximately 5–35 at.%; formulations containing 2 to less than 5 at.% Ge violate that boundary.
The rule equates less than a 10% yield-strength increase with absence of a statistically significant improvement, although an increase below 10% could still be statistically significant.
